title: The frontier fort (312–319)
hook: guard yourself like a border town, guarded within and without

segments.voice: Yesterday, kusa, and your line: grasp it right. What did you handle carefully, and did it feel different? Day two hundred fifteen, the second day of the downward course.

A capital city has big armies and thick walls. A town on the frontier has neither. It sits at the edge, where trouble arrives first, and the people there can't afford to be casual. They know which gate is weak, which stretch of wall is crumbling, which night the guards get sleepy. They check them all, every day, and inside the walls they keep order too. Today's verse takes a town like that as a picture of a person. Today: the frontier fort.
screen: `A TOWN AT THE EDGE.` → `TROUBLE ARRIVES FIRST.` → `THE WEAK GATE, THE SLEEPY GUARD.`

segments.voice: The chapter on the downward course keeps going with a run of plain advice. A slack effort, a vow half kept, a doubtful discipline: none of these brings much fruit. If something is worth doing, do it with your whole strength. A bad deed is better left undone, one verse says, because it burns you afterward; a good deed is better done, because it doesn't. Then comes verse three hundred fifteen, in Max Müller's English: "Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself." Within and without. The walls face outward, against what comes in through the senses: the ad, the insult, the easy temptation. But the fort also keeps watch inside, over the moods and thoughts that start their own trouble. The verse goes on: let no moment slip past, because those who let the right moment pass suffer for it later, in the downward course. The last verses of the chapter are a surprise. They're about shame and fear aimed at the wrong target. Some people are ashamed of what isn't shameful, and not ashamed of what is. Some fear what isn't dangerous, and shrug at what is. They see wrong where there is none and miss it where it is. So guarding the fort isn't the same as being anxious about everything. A good guard knows which gate is actually weak. Buddhist teaching has a name for this guarding, indriya-saṃvara: restraint of the senses, keeping watch at the doors of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind. It isn't a wall to hide behind. It's attention, placed where it's needed.
screen: `DO IT WITH YOUR WHOLE STRENGTH.` · `A FORT GUARDED WITHIN AND WITHOUT.` · `SHAME AND FEAR AT THE WRONG TARGET.` · `KNOW WHICH GATE IS WEAK.` · then, large: `GUARD THE BORDER TOWN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Walk the walls of your own town for a moment. Where does trouble usually get in for you? Maybe a gate on the outside: a certain app, a certain conversation, a certain time of night. Or a gate on the inside: a mood that turns sour, a thought that loops. Pick just one weak spot. Picture a calm guard standing there, not angry, just awake. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
The frontier fort. A border town guarded within and without: watch the gates of the senses, and the mind inside.
Your line: guard the border town. Today, guard the one weak spot you found, just for today, and notice how often trouble comes knocking at that gate. Day two hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners train in guarding the sense doors, noticing what comes in through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind; teachers often use the frontier-fort verse to describe it.

match.prompt: match each piece of today's verses.

myth: the fort only guards against things outside
the verse says within and without: the senses and the mind.
the chapter warns against fearing the wrong things
some fear what isn't dangerous and shrug at what is.
guarding the fort means being anxious about everything
a good guard knows which gate is actually weak.

fork.setup: you're the guard of a small frontier town. you can watch every gate a little, or learn which gate trouble really uses. what do today's verses point toward?
options: watch every gate in a panic.
know the weak gate, and guard within and without.
stay inside and never open a gate.
fork.reveal: the verses warn against fear aimed at the wrong target; the fort is guarded within and without, with attention where it's needed.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'the frontier fort' is about building walls to keep the world out.
what it means: guard yourself within and without: the senses coming in, the moods rising inside.
what a scholar hears: the Pali 'nagaram yatha paccantam' is a border city; the image matches the teaching of guarding the sense doors, indriya-samvara.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.quoted: Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hook rewritten (it opened 'Think of', and ended by telling the listener to be a fort); unsourced history line cut; verse 315's ending restored to the text's sense (suffering in the downward course, not just 'grieve later'); indriya-saṃvara named.
Müller's verse 315 verified exact against Gutenberg #2017 ('defences' is his spelling).
The hook's unsourced history line ('kingdoms kept towns like this along their borders') was cut; the Pali paccanta nagara (border city) is the verse's image.
original is null: 'paccanta nagara' could be added in Devanagari if a Keeper wants it.
